title: An Artist’s Impression
sub: Grades 5–8 Art · Our Incredible Moon · Evidence and imagination
objective: Students will read the art of the poster *Another Earth*: a violet-to-indigo night, lavender, pink and aqua; flat cartoon planets; an alien landscape of purple cliffs and three moons; a title in tall blocky letters. They will see how color, shape and lettering make a mood. Then they will set the art beside the poster’s facts about the planet HD 20794 d, which give its mass, its distance, its year and the shape of its orbit, but not its color. A picture of such a world is an **artist’s impression**: part evidence, part imagination. Students design one, and say which part is which.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Many pictures of other worlds are imagined. Knowing how an artist builds one, and where the facts stop, lets you enjoy the picture and still know what is real.

materials: Page 3 of this plan, projected or printed: the poster’s pictures, its palette, and the facts
Colored pencils or markers, with violet, pink and aqua if you have them; differentiated handouts, one per student
connection: **On the poster** *Another Earth*, find the ringed planet, the nebula and the landscape with three moons, then read the paragraph about HD 20794 d. Which parts of the poster are facts, and which are art?

steps.title: Where is this?
script: Show the landscape from the poster *Another Earth* for a full minute in silence. Ask: *“What do you notice first? Where is this?”* Take answers. Then: *“No one has ever been to a planet around another star. The poster says that with today’s technology, a trip to the planet HD 20794 d would take hundreds of thousands of years. So someone imagined this place. Today we ask how, and what an honest picture of another world would look like.”*

steps.purpose: Look before knowing: let the picture work, then ask where it came from.
students: Where is this place? How could anyone know what it looks like?

steps.title: Color, shape, lettering
script: **The look of the posters.** Show the moon from *Our Incredible Moon* and the ringed planet from *Another Earth*. The posters share a palette: a violet-to-indigo night, a lavender moon, white type, and on *Another Earth*, pink and aqua. The shapes are flat and simple, with smooth edges and soft shading. The title is set in tall blocky letters, pink above and white below. Ask what mood these choices make, and why an artist might choose a dreamy, cartoon style for worlds nobody has seen, rather than something that looks like a photograph.

steps.purpose: Name the artist’s choices and the mood they make.
students: Name the colors. Which do both posters share?
Are the shapes soft or sharp, simple or detailed?

steps.title: What we know
script: **What we know.** Read the poster’s facts about HD 20794 d and list them on the board (page 3). Then ask: *what color is it?* None of the facts says. The poster adds that such a planet *might lack the right atmosphere or have extreme temperatures*.

screen.text: Since then, over 6,000 exoplanets have been confirmed, including HD 20794 d, a “super-Earth” located about 20 light-years away in the constellation Eridanus. This planet is roughly six times the mass of Earth and orbits within its star’s habitable zone, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist. HD 20794 d takes about 647 days to circle its star. Its orbit is a stretched oval, so over its year it swings between the inner and outer edges of the habitable zone. Astronomers confirmed it in 2025, using more than 20 years of measurements.

steps.purpose: Collect the evidence: what the poster says about HD 20794 d.
students: List every fact about the planet.
Which fact tells you its color?

steps.title: Evidence or imagination?
script: **Evidence or imagination?** Name the term: an **artist’s impression** is a picture of something no one has seen, built from what is known and filled in with imagination. Fill in the chart together. Then show how scientists learn colors: the James Webb Space Telescope *reads the starlight that filters through a planet’s atmosphere, because different gases absorb different colors of light*. Colors read in starlight are evidence; colors in a painting, without such evidence, are imagination.

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three read the poster’s art, sort evidence from imagination, and design an impression of HD 20794 d with a caption.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Find the poster’s colors and name its mood. Sort six choices into evidence and imagination. Draw HD 20794 d with one fact and one imagined idea, labeled, and finish a caption.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Read the artist’s choices in a chart. Choose a palette for a mood. Design a landscape on HD 20794 d with three choices from evidence and three from imagination, and write the caption.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Judge whether the poster’s art makes the planet look more like home than the evidence allows. Show the planet at two points on its stretched orbit, and write an artist’s statement and an honest caption.

steps.purpose: Design an impression of HD 20794 d at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three end with a picture of your own, labeled evidence or imagination.

steps.title: Gallery walk
script: Lay the designs out as a gallery. Each student reads a classmate’s caption and points to one choice: evidence or imagination? Close with the question on the screen.

screen.question: If you could ask a scientist one question before you painted HD 20794 d, what would you ask?

steps.purpose: Read a classmate’s design: which choices are evidence, which imagination?
students: Point to one choice: evidence or imagination?

script: Ask the objectives back as questions: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down.
